claim: The SPI-22 T6SS of S. bongori is phylogenetically related to the HSI-III T6SS of P. aeruginosa with amino acid similarity ranging from 26% to 80%
source: The SPI-22 T6SS of S. bongori is phylogenetically related to the HSI-III (Hcp secretion island III) T6SS of P. aeruginosa (amino acid similarity ranging from 26% to 80%), and the CTS2 (Citrobacter rodentium T6SS cluster 2) of C. rodentium (amino acid similarity ranging from 63% to 93%) (Petty et al., 2010; Fookes et al., 2011; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by amino acid similarity data presented in the manuscript and referenced to prior publications (Petty et al., 2010; Fookes et al., 2011)

claim: The SPI-22 T6SS of S. bongori is phylogenetically related to the CTS2 of C. rodentium with amino acid similarity ranging from 63% to 93%
source: The SPI-22 T6SS of S. bongori is phylogenetically related to the HSI-III (Hcp secretion island III) T6SS of P. aeruginosa (amino acid similarity ranging from 26% to 80%), and the CTS2 (Citrobacter rodentium T6SS cluster 2) of C. rodentium (amino acid similarity ranging from 63% to 93%) (Petty et al., 2010; Fookes et al., 2011; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by amino acid similarity data presented in the manuscript and referenced to prior publications (Petty et al., 2010; Fookes et al., 2011)

claim: The genome of S. bongori NCTC 12419 encodes two VgrG proteins (SBG_2715, SBG_3770)
source: Besides the structural T6SS components encoded within SPI-22, the genome of S. bongori NCTC 12419 encodes several orphan proteins comprising two VgrG (SBG_2715, SBG_3770), four Hcp (SBG_0599, SBG_3120, SBG_3143, SBG_3925), three DUF4150/PAAR-like proteins (SBG_1846, SBG_2718, SBG_2955), two adaptors containing DUF2169 (SBG_1847, SBG_2721), and one adaptor with DUF1795 (SBG_3173) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on genomic data analysis of S. bongori NCTC 12419

claim: The genome of S. bongori NCTC 12419 encodes four Hcp proteins (SBG_0599, SBG_3120, SBG_3143, SBG_3925)
source: Besides the structural T6SS components encoded within SPI-22, the genome of S. bongori NCTC 12419 encodes several orphan proteins comprising two VgrG (SBG_2715, SBG_3770), four Hcp (SBG_0599, SBG_3120, SBG_3143, SBG_3925), three DUF4150/PAAR-like proteins (SBG_1846, SBG_2718, SBG_2955), two adaptors containing DUF2169 (SBG_1847, SBG_2721), and one adaptor with DUF1795 (SBG_3173) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on genomic data analysis of S. bongori NCTC 12419

claim: The genome of S. bongori NCTC 12419 encodes three DUF4150/PAAR-like proteins (SBG_1846, SBG_2718, SBG_2955)
source: Besides the structural T6SS components encoded within SPI-22, the genome of S. bongori NCTC 12419 encodes several orphan proteins comprising two VgrG (SBG_2715, SBG_3770), four Hcp (SBG_0599, SBG_3120, SBG_3143, SBG_3925), three DUF4150/PAAR-like proteins (SBG_1846, SBG_2718, SBG_2955), two adaptors containing DUF2169 (SBG_1847, SBG_2721), and one adaptor with DUF1795 (SBG_3173) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on genomic data analysis of S. bongori NCTC 12419

claim: The prey recovery rate was higher when coincubation was performed with ΔtssB compared to the WT S. bongori
source: Results showed that the prey recovery rate was higher when coincubation was performed with ΔtssB compared to the WT (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial competition assay data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Competition with a ΔtssB strain complemented with a plasmid expressing TssB restored the WT phenotype
source: In addition, competition with a ΔtssB strain complemented with a plasmid expressing TssB restored the WT phenotype (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial competition assay data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The SPI-22 T6SS of S. bongori is active in the conditions tested and contributes to interbacterial antagonism
source: These results show that the SPI-22 T6SS of S. bongori is active in the conditions tested and contributes to interbacterial antagonism, thus priming investigation to further characterize this activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the bacterial competition assay results showing differential prey recovery rates

claim: SBG_2718 (TseV1) contains an N-terminal PAAR-like domain and a C-terminal VRR-Nuc domain
source: Two candidates called our attention: SBG_2718 (TseV1) and SBG_2723 (TseV2), which contain an N-terminal PAAR-like domain and a C-terminal VRR-Nuc domain (Figure 2A; Kinch et al., 2005; Iyer et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on in silico domain analysis and supported by citations to prior work (Kinch et al., 2005; Iyer et al., 2006)

claim: SBG_2723 (TseV2) contains an N-terminal PAAR-like domain and a C-terminal VRR-Nuc domain
source: Two candidates called our attention: SBG_2718 (TseV1) and SBG_2723 (TseV2), which contain an N-terminal PAAR-like domain and a C-terminal VRR-Nuc domain (Figure 2A; Kinch et al., 2005; Iyer et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on in silico domain analysis and supported by citations to prior work (Kinch et al., 2005; Iyer et al., 2006)

claim: TseV1 is encoded next to two DUF3396-containing proteins (SBG_2719/TsiV1.1 and SBG_2720/TsiV1.2)
source: Both putative effectors are encoded next to pairs of genes encoding DUF3396-containing proteins that resemble putative immunity proteins: SBG_2719/TsiV1.1 and SBG_2720/TsiV1.2, and SBG_2724/TsiV2.1 and SBG_2725/TsiV2.2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on genomic context analysis

claim: TseV2 is encoded next to two DUF3396-containing proteins (SBG_2724/TsiV2.1 and SBG_2725/TsiV2.2)
source: Both putative effectors are encoded next to pairs of genes encoding DUF3396-containing proteins that resemble putative immunity proteins: SBG_2719/TsiV1.1 and SBG_2720/TsiV1.2, and SBG_2724/TsiV2.1 and SBG_2725/TsiV2.2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on genomic context analysis

claim: SBG_1841 (TseV3) contains an N-terminal PAAR-like domain
source: Additional BLASTP searches in the genome of S. bongori identified two extra VRR-Nuc-containing proteins (SBG_1841/TseV3 and SBG_1828/TseV4), but only one of them encodes an N-terminal PAAR-like domain (SBG_1841).
evidence: The claim is based on BLASTP search results and domain analysis

claim: SBG_1828 (TseV4) does not encode an N-terminal PAAR-like domain
source: Additional BLASTP searches in the genome of S. bongori identified two extra VRR-Nuc-containing proteins (SBG_1841/TseV3 and SBG_1828/TseV4), but only one of them encodes an N-terminal PAAR-like domain (SBG_1841).
evidence: The claim is based on BLASTP search results and domain analysis

claim: TseV3 is encoded upstream of a DUF3396-containing protein (SBG_1842/TsiV3)
source: Similarly, SBG_1828 and SBG_1841 are encoded upstream of a DUF3396-containing protein (SBG_1829/TsiV4 and SBG_1842/TsiV3) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on genomic context analysis

claim: TseV4 is encoded upstream of a DUF3396-containing protein (SBG_1829/TsiV4)
source: Similarly, SBG_1828 and SBG_1841 are encoded upstream of a DUF3396-containing protein (SBG_1829/TsiV4 and SBG_1842/TsiV3) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on genomic context analysis

claim: TseV2 is toxic when expressed in E. coli
source: Results showed that TseV2 and TseV3 are toxic in the cytoplasm of E. coli, whereas TseV1 and TseV4 do not confer toxicity (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 2B

claim: TseV3 is toxic when expressed in E. coli
source: Results showed that TseV2 and TseV3 are toxic in the cytoplasm of E. coli, whereas TseV1 and TseV4 do not confer toxicity (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 2B

claim: TseV1 does not confer toxicity when expressed in E. coli
source: Results showed that TseV2 and TseV3 are toxic in the cytoplasm of E. coli, whereas TseV1 and TseV4 do not confer toxicity (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 2B

claim: TseV4 does not confer toxicity when expressed in E. coli
source: Results showed that TseV2 and TseV3 are toxic in the cytoplasm of E. coli, whereas TseV1 and TseV4 do not confer toxicity (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Only TsiV2.1 neutralizes TseV2 toxicity
source: Coexpression of TseV2 with either TsiV2.1 or TsiV2.2 revealed that only the first immunity protein neutralizes TseV2 toxicity (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 2B

claim: TsiV3 neutralizes TseV3 toxicity
source: Similarly, the toxic effect of TseV3 can be neutralized by coexpression with TsiV3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 2B

claim: TseV2 and TseV3 are neutralized only by their specific cognate immunity proteins
source: Coexpression of TseV2 and TseV3 with all combinations of immunity proteins (TsiV1.1, TsiV1.2, TsiV2.1, TsiV2.2, TsiV3, and TsiV4) revealed that the effectors are neutralized only by the specific cognate immunity protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: E. coli carrying pBRA TseV2 stopped growing once l-arabinose was added
source: Under these conditions, bacteria grew normally in media containing d-glucose; but once l-arabinose was added, the culture stopped growing, and the OD600 nm stabilized (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2C

claim: E. coli carrying pBRA TseV3 stopped growing once l-arabinose was added
source: Under these conditions, bacteria grew normally in media containing d-glucose; but once l-arabinose was added, the culture stopped growing, and the OD600 nm stabilized (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2C

claim: E. coli expressing TseV2 or TseV3 did not grow and remained mostly morphologically unaltered in the presence of l-arabinose
source: However, in the presence of 0.2% l-arabinose (induced) bacteria did not grow and remained mostly morphologically unaltered – displaying a modest increase in cell length (Figure 2D, Figure 2—video 2, and Figure 2—video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and associated videos

claim: The prey recovery rate was higher when ΔtseV2/tsiV2.1/2.2 prey cells were coincubated with ΔtssB compared to WT S. bongori
source: Results demonstrated that the prey recovery rate was higher when prey cells were coincubated with ΔtssB compared to WT (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial competition assay data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Complementation of ΔtseV2/tsiV2.1/2.2 prey with a plasmid encoding TsiV2.1 increased the prey recovery rate
source: Complementation of preys with a plasmid encoding either TsiV2.1 or TsiV3 increased the prey recovery rate, showing that prey became immune to the TseV2- and TseV3-induced toxicity (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial competition assay data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Complementation of ΔtseV3/tsiV3 prey with a plasmid encoding TsiV3 increased the prey recovery rate
source: Complementation of preys with a plasmid encoding either TsiV2.1 or TsiV3 increased the prey recovery rate, showing that prey became immune to the TseV2- and TseV3-induced toxicity (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial competition assay data shown in Figure 2E

claim: TseV2 and TseV3 are antibacterial effectors secreted by the SPI-22 T6SS
source: These results confirm that TseV2 and TseV3 are antibacterial effectors secreted by the SPI-22 T6SS.
evidence: The claim is inferred from bacterial competition assay results showing that immunity proteins protect prey cells

claim: VgrG2 is responsible for secreting TseV2 into target cells
source: The prey recovery rate of ΔtseV2/tsiV2.1/2.2 increased when this strain was coincubated with ΔvgrG2, suggesting that VgrG2 is responsible for secreting TseV2 into target cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from bacterial competition assay data shown in Figure 2F

claim: VgrG3 is responsible for secreting TseV3 into target cells
source: Conversely, the prey recovery rate of ΔtseV3/tsiV3 increased when this strain was coincubated with ΔvgrG3, suggesting that VgrG3 is responsible for secreting TseV3 into target cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from bacterial competition assay data shown in Figure 2F

claim: VgrG2 and VgrG3 are 96.9% identical in their N-terminal region (VgrG21–565 and VgrG31–545)
source: VgrG2 and VgrG3 are 96.9% identical in their N-terminal region (VgrG21–565 and VgrG31–545), but display a distinct C-terminal domain with only 26% identity (VgrG2566–709 and VgrG3546–728) (Supplementary file 1), thus suggesting that this region is responsible for cargo selection (Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison data presented in Supplementary file 1

claim: VgrG2 and VgrG3 display a distinct C-terminal domain with only 26% identity (VgrG2566–709 and VgrG3546–728)
source: VgrG2 and VgrG3 are 96.9% identical in their N-terminal region (VgrG21–565 and VgrG31–545), but display a distinct C-terminal domain with only 26% identity (VgrG2566–709 and VgrG3546–728) (Supplementary file 1), thus suggesting that this region is responsible for cargo selection (Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison data presented in Supplementary file 1

claim: The C-terminal region of VgrG2 and VgrG3 is responsible for cargo selection
source: VgrG2 and VgrG3 are 96.9% identical in their N-terminal region (VgrG21–565 and VgrG31–545), but display a distinct C-terminal domain with only 26% identity (VgrG2566–709 and VgrG3546–728) (Supplementary file 1), thus suggesting that this region is responsible for cargo selection (Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is inferred from sequence comparison data and supported by citation to Liang et al., 2021

claim: VRR-Nuc domain was initially annotated as DUF994
source: TseV2 and TseV3 contain a VRR-Nuc domain at their C-terminus, which was initially annotated as DUF994 (Kinch et al., 2005) and later renamed VRR-Nuc due to its association with enzymes linked to DNA metabolism (Iyer et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kinch et al., 2005; Iyer et al., 2006)

claim: VRR-Nuc domain was renamed from DUF994 due to its association with enzymes linked to DNA metabolism
source: TseV2 and TseV3 contain a VRR-Nuc domain at their C-terminus, which was initially annotated as DUF994 (Kinch et al., 2005) and later renamed VRR-Nuc due to its association with enzymes linked to DNA metabolism (Iyer et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kinch et al., 2005; Iyer et al., 2006)

claim: VRR-Nuc-containing proteins are found in bacteria, bacteriophages, fungi, and eukaryotes
source: VRR-Nuc-containing proteins are found in a wide range of organisms, including bacteria, bacteriophages, fungi, and eukaryotes (Iyer et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Iyer et al., 2006

claim: Proteins containing the VRR-Nuc domain comprise a family (PF08774) belonging to the PD-(D/E)xK superfamily
source: Proteins containing this domain comprise a family (PF08774) belonging to the PD-(D/E)xK superfamily, which constitutes a large and functionally diverse group containing representatives involved in DNA replication (Holliday junction resolvases), restriction–modification, repair, and tRNA-intron splicing (Steczkiewicz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Steczkiewicz et al., 2012

claim: Members of the PD-(D/E)xK superfamily exhibit low sequence similarity but display a common fold in their enzymatic core (with α1β1β2β3α2β4 topology)
source: Members of this superfamily exhibit low sequence similarity but display a common fold in their enzymatic core (with α1β1β2β3α2β4 topology), which contains conserved residues (Asp, Glu, and Lys) responsible for catalysis (Steczkiewicz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Steczkiewicz et al., 2012

claim: The enzymatic core of PD-(D/E)xK superfamily members contains conserved residues (Asp, Glu, and Lys) responsible for catalysis
source: Members of this superfamily exhibit low sequence similarity but display a common fold in their enzymatic core (with α1β1β2β3α2β4 topology), which contains conserved residues (Asp, Glu, and Lys) responsible for catalysis (Steczkiewicz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Steczkiewicz et al., 2012

claim: Antibacterial T6SS effectors (TseVs, Aave_0499, IdrD, and PoNe) formed a clade with a bootstrap value higher than 75%
source: All T6SS effectors (TseVs, Aave_0499, IdrD, and PoNe), except for TseT homologs, formed a clade with a bootstrap value higher than 75% (Figure 3A, colors).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The genomic context of TseV/Plu1493 homologs is enriched in proteins encoding components of the T6SS apparatus, adaptors, and immunity proteins
source: While most of VRR-Nuc members (PmgM, T1p21, KIAA1018, Bce1019, and HP1472) are encoded next to genes involved in DNA metabolism, the gene neighborhood of antibacterial T6SS effectors (TseVs, Aave_0499, IdrD, and PoNe) is enriched in proteins encoding components of the T6SS apparatus, adaptors, and immunity proteins (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is based on genomic context analysis shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3

claim: Substitution of the conserved aspartic acid for alanine in TseV2 (TseV2D282A) abrogated toxicity in E. coli
source: Using this information as a guide, substitution of the conserved aspartic acid for alanine in TseV2 (TseV2D282A) and TseV3 (TseV3D230A) abrogated toxicity in E. coli (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Substitution of the conserved aspartic acid for alanine in TseV3 (TseV3D230A) abrogated toxicity in E. coli
source: Using this information as a guide, substitution of the conserved aspartic acid for alanine in TseV2 (TseV2D282A) and TseV3 (TseV3D230A) abrogated toxicity in E. coli (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The enzymatic activity of the VRR-Nuc domain is essential for toxicity
source: These results confirm that the enzymatic activity of the VRR-Nuc domain is essential for toxicity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mutagenesis data showing that catalytic mutants are not toxic

claim: E. coli expressing TseV2 or TseV3 showed an increase in GFP fluorescence when expression was induced with l-arabinose, indicating activation of the SOS response
source: We observed an increase in GFP fluorescence when the expression of TseV2 or TseV3 was induced with l-arabinose, indicating the activation of the SOS response (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SOS response reporter assay data shown in Figure 4A and 4B

claim: Cells expressing TseV2 or TseV3 revealed smaller/degraded nucleoids and displayed reduced DAPI fluorescence
source: Cells expressing TseV2 or TseV3 revealed smaller/degraded nucleoids and displayed reduced DAPI fluorescence (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by DAPI staining data shown in Figure 4C-F

claim: E. coli expressing either TseV2 or TseV3 revealed several intense GFP foci in more than 80% and 75% of cells, respectively
source: Conversely, E. coli expressing either TseV2 or TseV3 revealed several intense GFP foci in more than 80% and 75% of cells, respectively (Figure 4G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by GamGFP double-strand break assay data shown in Figure 4G and 4H

claim: The expression of the catalytic mutants TseV2D282A and TseV3D230A did not induce GFP foci formation
source: The expression of the catalytic mutants TseV2D282A and TseV3D230A did not induce GFP foci formation, indicating that the observed phenotype is specific to the effector's enzymatic activity (Figure 4G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by GamGFP double-strand break assay data shown in Figure 4G and 4H

claim: TseV2 and TseV3 cause target cell death by inducing DNA double-strand breaks
source: Together, these results suggest that TseV2 and TseV3 cause target cell death by inducing DNA double-strand breaks.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results including SOS response activation, nucleoid degradation, and GamGFP foci formation

claim: VRR-Nuc-containing enzymes have been shown to be specific for certain DNA structures rather than sequences in eukaryotes
source: VRR-Nuc-containing enzymes have been shown to be specific for certain DNA structures rather than sequences, both in eukaryotes (Kratz et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2010; MacKay et al., 2010; Smogorzewska et al., 2010) and prokaryotes (Gwon et al., 2014; Pennell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kratz et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2010; MacKay et al., 2010; Smogorzewska et al., 2010)

claim: VRR-Nuc-containing enzymes have been shown to be specific for certain DNA structures rather than sequences in prokaryotes
source: VRR-Nuc-containing enzymes have been shown to be specific for certain DNA structures rather than sequences, both in eukaryotes (Kratz et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2010; MacKay et al., 2010; Smogorzewska et al., 2010) and prokaryotes (Gwon et al., 2014; Pennell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Gwon et al., 2014; Pennell et al., 2014)

claim: The preferred DNA structure for human FAN1 and P. aeruginosa PaFAN1 is a 5′ flap
source: In these cases, the prefered DNA structure is a 5′ flap (Gwon et al., 2014) – a Y-shaped DNA form in which one of the arms (5′) is a single strand and the other (3′) is a double strand.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gwon et al., 2014

claim: In both human FAN1 and P. aeruginosa PaFAN1, the 5′ flap is cleaved a couple of nucleotides (1–5 nt) downstream from the arms junction
source: In both human FAN1 and P. aeruginosa PaFAN1, the 5′ flap is cleaved a couple of nucleotides (1–5 nt) downstream from the arms junction and later the opposite strand is cleaved creating a double-strand end (Gwon et al., 2014; Pennell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Gwon et al., 2014; Pennell et al., 2014)

claim: FAN1 enzymes display 5′–3′ exonuclease activity
source: Besides endonuclease activity, FAN1 enzymes also display 5′–3′ exonuclease activity (Kratz et al., 2010; Gwon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kratz et al., 2010; Gwon et al., 2014)

claim: TseV3 preferentially cleaves the splayed arm substrate, with some minor activity on the 3′ flap substrate
source: Results revealed that TseV3 preferentially cleaves the splayed arm substrate, with some minor activity on the 3′ flap substrate (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: No degradation was detected for the catalytic mutant TseV3D230A
source: The activity was specific as no degradation was detected for the catalytic mutant TseV3D230A (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Human FAN1 and P. aeruginosa PaFAN1 are metal-dependent nucleases that use Mn2+ as a cofactor
source: Human FAN1 and P. aeruginosa PaFAN1 are metal-dependent nucleases that use Mn2+ as a cofactor (Kratz et al., 2010; Gwon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kratz et al., 2010; Gwon et al., 2014)

claim: TseV3 requires Mn2+ as a cofactor
source: Results revealed that TseV3 requires Mn2+ as a cofactor, and its activity was inhibited by EDTA and partially affected by Zn2+ (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: TseV3 activity was inhibited by EDTA
source: Results revealed that TseV3 requires Mn2+ as a cofactor, and its activity was inhibited by EDTA and partially affected by Zn2+ (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: TseV3 activity was partially affected by Zn2+
source: Results revealed that TseV3 requires Mn2+ as a cofactor, and its activity was inhibited by EDTA and partially affected by Zn2+ (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: TseV3 cleaves the splayed arm at variable distances after the arms junction
source: In agreement with the reported activity of FAN1 and PaFAN1, we observed the appearance of a range of fragments around 35-mer, suggesting that TseV3 cleaves the splayed arm at variable distances after the arms junction (Figure 5C), thus resembling what is observed for PaFAN1 in 5′ flap that cleaves the third to fifth nucleotide downstream from the junction (Gwon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from time-course degradation assay data shown in Figure 5C and comparison with PaFAN1 activity

claim: TseV3 displays a unique activity and behaves as a structure-specific nuclease
source: Together, these results confirm that TseV3 displays a unique activity and behaves as a structure-specific nuclease.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple in vitro enzymatic assay results

claim: The MALS calculated average mass for the TseV3:TsiV3 complex was 66.4 ± 3.3 kDa
source: The MALS calculated average mass for the complex was 66.4 ± 3.3 kDa, which is close to the sum of the theoretical values of their monomers: 26.8 and 37.4 kDa for 6xHis-TseV3 and TsiV3, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data

claim: TseV3 and TsiV3 form a 1:1 heterodimeric complex
source: These results reveal that TseV3 and TsiV form a 1:1 heterodimeric complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from SEC-MALS data showing the molecular mass of the complex

claim: Crystals of the TseV3:TsiV3 complex belong to space group P21 and diffracted to a moderate resolution of 4 Å
source: We were able to obtain crystals of the TseV3:TsiV3 complex, which belong to space group P21 and diffracted to a moderate resolution of 4 Å (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is based on X-ray crystallography data

claim: Matthews coefficient analysis indicated that two TseV3:TsiV3 complexes would be the most likely composition in the asymmetric unit
source: Matthews coefficient analysis indicated that two TseV3:TsiV3 complexes would be the most likely composition in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: The claim is based on crystallographic analysis

claim: Molecular replacement using AlphaFold models of TseV3132–281 and TsiV310–327 was able to place two copies of each monomer in the asymmetric unit with a final LLG of 486.87 and TFZ of 12.4
source: We used AlphaFold (Jumper et al., 2021) models of TseV3132–281 and TsiV310–327 for molecular replacement using Phaser (McCoy et al., 2007), which was able to place two copies of each monomer in the asymmetric unit with a final LLG (log-likelihood gain) of 486.87 and TFZ (translation function Z-score) of 12.4 – with both heterodimeric complexes adopting the same pose (our docked model is available using accession code ma-oyho8 at modelarchive.org).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular replacement analysis using AlphaFold models

claim: TsiV3 possesses a central β-sheet that is flanked by α-helices on one side and exposed on the other
source: TsiV3 possesses a central β-sheet that is flanked by α-helices on one side and exposed on the other (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the TseV3:TsiV3 complex model

claim: The exposed β-sheet surface of TsiV3 binds to an α–β element of TseV3 that flanks its putative active site
source: This exposed β-sheet surface of TsiV3 binds to an α–β element of TseV3 that flanks its putative active site (composed of residues D230, D245, and K247) (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the TseV3:TsiV3 complex model

claim: TsiV3L131K was unable to neutralize TseV3 toxicity
source: Results revealed that TsiV3L131K was unable to neutralize TseV3 toxicity.
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data

claim: TseV3P256K maintained its enzymatic activity, displaying toxicity in E. coli
source: In addition, the mutated TseV3P256K maintained its enzymatic activity, displaying toxicity in E. coli; however, this mutant was not neutralized by coexpression with the native immunity protein (TsiV3) (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 6C

claim: TseV3P256K was not neutralized by coexpression with the native immunity protein (TsiV3)
source: In addition, the mutated TseV3P256K maintained its enzymatic activity, displaying toxicity in E. coli; however, this mutant was not neutralized by coexpression with the native immunity protein (TsiV3) (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by E. coli toxicity assay data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Residues D230, D245, and K247 of TseV3 match residues D507, E522, and K524 of PaFAN1
source: Accordingly, superimposition of TseV3 with the well-characterized VRR-Nuc member PaFAN1 (PDB 4R89) (Gwon et al., 2014) (clade KIAA1018 in Figure 3A) matches residues D230, D245, and K247 of the former with residues D507, E522, and K524 of the latter (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is based on structural superimposition analysis

claim: The path of the DNA substrate is potentially incompatible with the presence of TsiV3 in the TseV3:TsiV3 complex
source: Comparison between the PaFAN1:DNA and TseV3:TsiV3 complexes reveals that the path of the DNA substrate is potentially incompatible with the presence of TsiV3 (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural comparison between PaFAN1:DNA and TseV3:TsiV3 complexes

claim: The binding of TsiV3 sterically blocks the TseV3 active site
source: Hence, assuming the mode of substrate recognition is similar between PaFAN1 and TseV3, this result suggests that the binding of TsiV3 sterically blocks the toxin active site.
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural comparison and assumes similar substrate recognition modes

claim: TsiV3 occlusion of the TseV3 active site would be enabled by a TsiV3 loop, which projects into the putative TseV3 DNA-binding pocket
source: In our model of the complex, TsiV3 occlusion of the TseV3 active site would be enabled by a TsiV3 loop, which projects into the putative TseV3 DNA-binding pocket (Figure 6A, D).
evidence: The claim is based on structural model analysis

claim: TseV effectors are the first example of effectors with a structure-specific nuclease activity
source: In this study, we characterized a group of effectors containing the VRR-Nuc domain, which comprise the first example of effectors with a structure-specific nuclease activity.
evidence: The claim is based on the characterization of TseV effectors and comparison with previously reported effectors

claim: The VRR-Nuc domain has not previously been reported to be used in biological conflicts
source: This domain has not previously been reported to be used in biological conflicts (Zhang et al., 2012), but recently was suggested to work as a T6SS effector due to its localization next to a PAAR protein in P. aeruginosa (Wang et al., 2021) – for consistency we decided to keep the name TseV for this group of effectors.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Zhang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2021)

claim: TseV3 acts on replication forks or transcription bubbles of target cells
source: Given the biochemical evidence suggesting that TseV3 cleaves splayed arms, we hypothesize that TseV3 acts on replication forks or transcription bubbles of target cells.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on biochemical evidence of TseV3 substrate specificity

claim: TseV3 activity on replication forks could promote the collapse of the replication machinery, thus inducing double-strand breaks
source: The effector activity could be directly responsible for creating the double-strand breaks detected in the GamGFP reporter assay, which can detect up to a four-base single-strand DNA overhang (Akroyd and Symonds, 1986; Shee et al., 2013); or its activity on replication forks could promote the collapse of the replication machinery, thus inducing double-strand breaks (Kuzminov, 1999).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work (Akroyd and Symonds, 1986; Shee et al., 2013; Kuzminov, 1999)

claim: Most T6SS immunity proteins bind to effectors to regulate their enzymatic activity
source: Most T6SS immunity proteins described to date bind to effectors to regulate their enzymatic activity (Benz et al., 2012; Benz et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2014; Robb et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Benz et al., 2012; Benz et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2014; Robb et al., 2016)

claim: Tri1 from Serratia proteamaculans exhibits two modes of inhibition: active site occlusion and enzymatic removal of a post-translational modification
source: An exception is Tri1 (type VI secretion ADP-ribosyltransferase immunity 1) from Serratia proteamaculans, which exhibits two modes of inhibition: active site occlusion and enzymatic removal of a post-translational modification (Ting et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ting et al., 2018

claim: TsiT interferes with TseT oligomerization state and hinders its nuclease activity
source: The neutralization mechanism of TsiT, which counteracts the PD-(D/E)xK effector TseT from P. aeruginosa, was also proposed to be different: TsiT interferes with the effector oligomerization state and hinders its nuclease activity (Wen et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wen et al., 2021

claim: TsiV3 β-sheet binds to the α2-helix of TseV3, which is involved in DNA binding in other PD-(D/E)xK members
source: Our structural model of the TseV3:TsiV3 complex revealed that TsiV3 β-sheet binds to the α2-helix of TseV3, which is involved in DNA binding in other PD-(D/E)xK members (Steczkiewicz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on structural model analysis and supported by citation to Steczkiewicz et al., 2012

claim: TsiV3 likely occludes the substrate-binding site of TseV3
source: In addition, the superposition of the TseV3:TsiV3 complex with the structure of PaFAN1 bound to DNA reinforces the hypothesis that TsiV3 likely occludes the substrate-binding site of TseV3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural superposition analysis
